items.title: An atom of carbon-14 is chemically identical to carbon-12
items.claim: Carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 are all carbon. They have 6 protons and react chemically the same way. They differ only in the number of neutrons — and one of them (C-14) is radioactive.
items.prompt: Why does chemistry not distinguish isotopes?

options.text: Isotopes are too rare to matter
Chemistry is governed by the electron arrangement, which depends on the number of protons (atomic number) — neutrons add mass but do not affect the electron shells that control bonding
Isotopes are the same element with the same number of neutrons

items.reveal_title: Atomic number defines the element, mass number distinguishes isotopes
items.reveal:
Nuclide notation: write the mass number A (protons + neutrons) as a superscript and atomic number Z (protons) as a subscript before the symbol. C-14 has Z=6, A=14, so it has 8 neutrons.

Because electron configuration depends only on Z, all carbon isotopes share the same chemical behaviour. They differ in mass, nuclear stability, and very slightly in reaction rates (kinetic isotope effects — useful for mechanism studies).

C-14 is radioactive with a half-life of 5730 years and decays by beta emission to N-14. Its constant atmospheric concentration (produced by cosmic rays in the upper atmosphere) underwrites radiocarbon dating of organic remains up to about 50,000 years old.
items.why: Students often confuse isotopes with different elements. The proton count is what 'makes' the element; neutrons are bookkeeping for the nucleus.

items.title: The hardest known natural substance and a pencil lead are the same element
items.claim: Diamond scores 10 on the Mohs hardness scale. Graphite scores 1-2 (it leaves a streak on paper). Both are 100 percent pure carbon. Same element, same atoms, vastly different materials.

options.text: Diamond is sp3 hybridised with every carbon bonded tetrahedrally to four others (a rigid 3D network); graphite is sp2 with strong in-plane bonds but only weak van der Waals forces between layers
Diamond and graphite have different isotopes of carbon

items.reveal:
In diamond every carbon shares electrons with four neighbours arranged at 109.5 degrees. The result is a giant covalent lattice that cannot be deformed without breaking strong sigma bonds in many directions at once.

In graphite each carbon bonds strongly to three neighbours in a flat hexagonal sheet. Sheets stack but are held together only by weak dispersion forces. Layers slide past each other easily — hence the pencil-streak behaviour.

Thermodynamically, graphite is actually the more stable form at room temperature and pressure by 2.9 kJ/mol. Diamond is metastable — it would convert to graphite, given long enough.
items.why: Identity of an element is not enough to determine properties. Bonding arrangement (allotropy) can transform a substance utterly.

items.title: You can buy crystals of a 'noble gas' compound by the gram
items.claim: Xenon difluoride (XeF2) is sold by chemical suppliers. Xenon tetrafluoride (XeF4) was first synthesised in 1962 by Claassen, Selig and Malm at Argonne National Lab. The textbook claim that noble gases 'do not react' was overturned 60 years ago.
items.prompt: What made xenon chemistry possible in 1962?

options.text: Neil Bartlett at UBC noticed xenon's first ionisation energy (1170 kJ/mol) is almost identical to O2's (1175 kJ/mol). Since PtF6 oxidised O2, he tried Xe + PtF6 — and got XePtF6, the first noble gas compound
Lasers were finally powerful enough to break Xe bonds

items.reveal:
In early 1962 Bartlett had been making PtF6 — a brilliant red solid — and noticed a sample turned red on contact with air. Analysis showed O2+ PtF6-: PtF6 had stripped an electron from O2.

Bartlett looked up xenon's first ionisation energy and saw the near-equality with O2. He reasoned that PtF6 should also oxidise Xe. The synthesis of yellow XePtF6 made the front page of Chemical & Engineering News.

Within months Claassen, Selig and Malm at Argonne produced XeF4 by simply heating Xe and F2 in a nickel container at 400°C. Today there are dozens of xenon compounds (XeO3, XeO4, XeF6, KrF2, ArF — the last only at cryogenic temperatures).

Helium and neon remain genuinely unreactive in normal conditions — their ionisation energies (2080 and 2370 kJ/mol) are too high for any known oxidiser to defeat.
items.why: 'Inert' is a useful summary, not a law of nature. Strong enough chemistry breaks even the rule of full octets.
